title: Rare events in a fixed window
objectives: Obtain the Poisson distribution as a limit of the binomial
Use $e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k/k!$ for counts in a fixed window
Recognise when clustering rules the Poisson out

screens.title: Rare events in a fixed window
screens.prose: A desk sees about 2 large orders an hour, and they arrive at random moments. Counting them is a binomial with many tiny trials. We will find what that binomial becomes.
Model the hour as 10 six-minute slots. Each slot holds a large order with chance 0.2, independently, and never more than one. The count is $\text{Bin}(10, 0.2)$, with mean $10 \times 0.2 = 2$.
screens.question: What is the chance of no large order in the whole hour?

hints.text: No order in the hour means every slot is empty.
Each slot is empty with chance 0.8.
Ten empty slots: $0.8^{10}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Every one of the 10 slots must be empty.

byKey.mean-two: A mean of 2 is an average over many hours. Some hours have none.
byKey.one-slot: 0.8 is the chance one slot is empty. All ten must be empty.
byKey.all: $0.2^{10}$ is the chance every slot has an order. You want every slot empty.

explain.text: All ten slots are empty with chance $0.8^{10} \approx 0.1074$. But real orders do not keep to six-minute slots. Two could land in one slot, so we should cut the hour finer.

screens.prose: Cut the hour into $n$ slots, each with chance $p = 2/n$, so the mean stays at 2. The bars are $\text{Bin}(n, 2/n)$. The dashed line is a fixed curve we will name shortly. Slide $n$ from 10 to 500.
screens.question: As $n$ grows, what does $P(X = 0)$ settle near?

options.why: You expected more slots to mean more chances of an order. But each slot's chance shrinks, so the mean stays at 2.
Read the caption as you slide: $P(X = 0)$ climbs from 0.1074 and then levels off.
Each slot is almost always empty, but there are very many slots. Together they still average 2 orders.

hints.text: Watch the caption's $P(X = 0)$ as you slide to the right.
At $n = 500$ the bars sit on the dashed curve.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide $n$ up to 500 and read $P(X = 0)$ from the caption.

explain.text: $(1 - 2/n)^n$ rises from 0.1074 at $n = 10$ to 0.1299 at 50 and 0.1348 at 500. Its limit is $e^{-2} \approx 0.1353$. Every other bar settles onto the dashed curve too.

screens.prose: The dashed curve is the **Poisson distribution** with rate $\lambda = np = 2$: $$P(X = k) = \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k}{k!}, \quad k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$$ It counts events in a fixed window when they are rare and independent. $\lambda$ is the mean count per window.
screens.question: What is $P(X = 2)$?

hints.text: Put $\lambda = 2$ and $k = 2$ into the formula.
$e^{-2} \approx 0.1353$ is the bar at 0.

byKey.ten-slots: 0.302 is $P(X = 2)$ for $\text{Bin}(10, 0.2)$, the coarse ten-slot model.
byKey.no-factorial: You left out the $k! = 2$ on the bottom.

explain.text: $P(X = 2) = e^{-2} \times 2^2 / 2! \approx 0.2707$. The binomial with 500 slots gave 0.2712, already close. Notice $P(X = 1) = P(X = 2)$ when $\lambda = 2$.

screens.prose: A code base averages 1.5 bugs per 1,000 lines, and bugs appear independently. Model the bugs in a new 1,000-line module as $\text{Pois}(1.5)$.
screens.question: What is the chance the module has no bugs?

hints.text: Put $k = 0$ into the formula.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. With $k = 0$ the formula leaves only $e^{-\lambda}$.

byKey.e-one: $e^{-1}$ drops the rate. The exponent is $-\lambda = -1.5$.
byKey.zero: A mean of 1.5 does not force a bug. About one module in five is clean.

explain.text: With $k = 0$, $\lambda^0 / 0! = 1$, so $P(X = 0) = e^{-\lambda} = e^{-1.5} \approx 0.2231$. The chance of no event at all is always $e^{-\lambda}$. It shrinks fast as $\lambda$ grows.

screens.prose: Back to the orders. $\text{Bin}(n, 2/n)$ has mean 2 for every $n$. Its variance is $np(1 - p) = 2(1 - 2/n)$: 1.6 at $n = 10$ and 1.992 at $n = 500$.
screens.question: What is the variance of the Poisson limit, $\text{Pois}(2)$?

hints.text: What happens to $2/n$ as $n$ grows?
$1 - 2/n$ tends to 1.

feedback.correct: The variance tends to 2, the same as the mean.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Let $n$ grow in $2(1 - 2/n)$.

byKey.vanish: Each slot's chance goes to 0, but there are ever more slots. The variance tends to $2 \times 1$, not 0.
byKey.ten: 1.6 is the ten-slot variance. Let $n$ grow.
byKey.sd: 1.414 is $\sqrt{2}$, the standard deviation. The variance itself is 2.

explain.text: As $n \to \infty$, $2(1 - 2/n) \to 2$. So a Poisson count has mean and variance both equal to $\lambda$. Its standard deviation is $\sqrt{\lambda} \approx 1.414$ here.

screens.prose: A fund gets margin calls at an average rate of 0.5 a year, independently over time. A colleague says the chance of a margin call this year is therefore 0.5.
screens.question: What is the chance of at least one margin call this year?

options.why: You read the rate $\lambda$ as a probability. $\lambda$ is a mean count; some years have two or more calls.
That is the chance of no margin call. You want at least one, its complement.
That is the chance of exactly one call. Years with two or more also count.

hints.text: $\lambda = 0.5$ is the mean number of calls, not a chance.
At least one is the complement of none.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $P(X = 0)$ first, then take its complement.

byKey.rate: You used the rate as a chance. A rate of 0.5 includes years with two or three calls, so the chance of any call is lower.

explain.text: $P(X \ge 1) = 1 - e^{-0.5} \approx 0.3935$. The rate 0.5 counts every call, and some years bring two or more. So the chance of at least one is below $\lambda$; a rate can even exceed 1.

screens.prose: Now the limit in general. Take $\text{Bin}(n, p)$ with $p = \lambda/n$, and fix $k$ while $n \to \infty$.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $= \dfrac{n(n - 1)\cdots(n - k + 1)}{n^k} \cdot \dfrac{\lambda^k}{k!} \cdot \left(1 - \dfrac{\lambda}{n}\right)^{n}\left(1 - \dfrac{\lambda}{n}\right)^{-k}$: write out $\binom{n}{k}$ and split the power.
The first fraction tends to 1: it is $k$ factors, each $(n - j)/n \to 1$.

hints.text: Start from the binomial you already know.
Rewrite before taking limits: the split line makes each factor's limit easy.
Binomial, split, first fraction to 1, the powers to $e^{-\lambda}$ and 1, multiply.

feedback.correct: Each factor has a simple limit, and the product of the limits is the Poisson pmf.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write the binomial first, rearrange it, then take each factor's limit.

byKey.end: The product of the limits comes last, once each factor's limit is known.
byKey.split: Rearranging uses the binomial line, so it comes second.

explain.text: You saw $(1 - 2/n)^n \to e^{-2}$ on the slider; the same limit drives every $k$. The counting factor $\binom{n}{k}/n^k$ becomes $1/k!$. So many independent rare chances add up to a Poisson count.

screens.prose: A block-trading desk sees 3 large orders an hour on average, arriving independently. A risk manager wants the chance of a busy hour with 6 or more. The shading shows $P(X \le 5)$ for $\text{Pois}(3)$.
screens.question: What is the chance of 6 or more large orders in an hour?

hints.text: 6 or more is everything outside the shading.
The shaded bars, 0 to 5, sum to 0.9161.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take 1 minus the shaded probability.

byKey.complement: 0.9161 is $P(X \le 5)$, the shaded part. You want the rest.
byKey.six-only: 0.0504 is $P(X = 6)$ alone. 7, 8 and more also count.
byKey.five: 0.1008 is $P(X = 5)$. The busy hour starts at 6.

explain.text: $P(X \ge 6) = 1 - P(X \le 5) \approx 0.0839$. So about one hour in twelve is that busy. Staff the desk for it, or route the extra orders.

screens.prose: You count large price jumps in a stock each day for a year. The counts average 2 a day, but the table shows how they spread. Poisson(2) would give a 6-jump day a chance of about 0.017.
screens.question: Is $\text{Pois}(2)$ a safe model for days with many jumps?

options.text: No: the variance is three times the mean, so jumps cluster and big days are far more common
Yes: the mean is 2, and that is all a Poisson needs
options.why: You matched the mean only. A Poisson also forces the variance to equal the mean, and here it is 6.1.

options.text: Yes: jumps are rare, so the Poisson always applies
options.why: Rare is not enough. The events must also be independent, and clustered jumps are not.

options.text: No: a Poisson needs the variance below the mean
options.why: You have the condition backwards. A Poisson has variance exactly equal to its mean.

hints.text: For a Poisson, how do the mean and variance compare?
Compare 2.0 with 6.1.
A variance well above the mean means events arrive in bursts, not independently.

feedback.correct: Variance above the mean is the sign of clustering, called overdispersion.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the Poisson's rule that variance equals mean.

explain.text: Poisson(2) predicts 6 or more jumps on about $250 \times 0.0166 \approx 4$ days, but there were 21. Jumps arrive in bursts after news, so they are not independent. Variance above the mean, overdispersion, is the warning sign.

ideas: Many independent trials, each with a tiny chance, with mean $np = \lambda$ fixed, give a Poisson count.
$P(X = k) = e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k/k!$, so the chance of no event is $e^{-\lambda}$.
A Poisson has mean and variance both $\lambda$. Variance well above the mean signals clustering.

formula.name: Poisson distribution
formula.note: $\lambda$ is the mean count per window: a rate, not a probability.

summary.trap: A rate of 0.5 a year is not a 0.5 chance of an event: it is $1 - e^{-0.5} \approx 0.39$.

quiz.prose: A system raises alerts at an average rate of 4 a day, independently.
quiz.question: What is the chance of a day with no alerts?

byKey.rate: You divided 1 by the rate. The chance of none is $e^{-4}$.

explain.text: With $k = 0$ the Poisson formula leaves $e^{-\lambda}$. Here $e^{-4} \approx 0.0183$. A quiet day happens about once in 55 days.

quiz.prose: Defaults in a large loan book are modelled as $\text{Pois}(2.5)$ per year.
quiz.question: What is the variance of the yearly number of defaults?

options.why: 1.58 is $\sqrt{2.5}$, the standard deviation. The variance equals $\lambda$ itself.
You squared $\lambda$. For a Poisson the variance is $\lambda$, not $\lambda^2$.

options.text: Close to 0, since each loan rarely defaults
options.why: Each loan is rare, but the total count still varies. Its variance is $\lambda = 2.5$.

feedback.correct: Mean and variance of a Poisson are both $\lambda$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall what the Poisson's variance equals.

explain.text: $\text{Var}(X) = \lambda = 2.5$ for a Poisson. It is the limit of $np(1 - p)$ with $p \to 0$. The standard deviation is $\sqrt{2.5} \approx 1.58$ defaults.

quiz.prose: A strategy sends 1,000 orders a day. Each is rejected by the exchange with chance 0.002, independently.
quiz.question: Using a Poisson approximation, what is the chance of exactly one rejection in a day?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set $\lambda = np$, then use $k = 1$.

byKey.zero: 0.1353 is the chance of no rejection. Multiply by $\lambda^1/1! = 2$.
byKey.lambda: 2 is the mean number of rejections, not a chance.
byKey.p: 0.002 is one order's chance. You want the chance of exactly one among 1,000.

explain.text: $\lambda = np = 2$, so $P(X = 1) \approx 2e^{-2} \approx 0.2707$. The exact binomial gives 0.2707 too, to four places. Large $n$ and small $p$ make the approximation excellent.

quiz.prose: Large orders arrive at 3 an hour on average, independently. Consider a 20-minute window.
quiz.question: What is the chance of no large order in those 20 minutes?

widget.accept: 0.3679: $\lambda = 1$ for a third of an hour, $e^{-1}$
widget.label: Chance of no order in 20 minutes

feedback.correct: Twenty minutes carries a third of the hourly rate: $e^{-1} \approx 0.3679$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Scale $\lambda$ to the window first.

byKey.hour: $e^{-3}$ is for a whole hour. A 20-minute window has $\lambda = 1$.
byKey.third: You divided the hour's answer by 3. Scale the rate, not the probability.
byKey.linear: You took $1 - 1/3$. The chance of none is $e^{-\lambda}$ with $\lambda = 1$.

explain.text: The rate scales with the window: $3 \times \tfrac{1}{3} = 1$ order per 20 minutes. So $P(X = 0) = e^{-1} \approx 0.3679$. Always match $\lambda$ to the window you are counting in.
